turns.content: My best friend Shreya's wedding festivities got dated — and her sangeet plus cocktail night is smack in the middle of Ramzan. I'll be fasting. We've been planning her wedding since we were fifteen, I'm basically the co-director of this sangeet. She keeps saying "you HAVE to do the opening dance with me." I want to. And I'm dreading all of it.

Oh, that sounds genuinely hard — because it’s not just “a party during fasting,” it’s *Shreya’s wedding*, the friend you’ve imagined this with forever, and a role you’ve emotionally carried for years. Of course part of you wants to say yes. And of course another part of you is already exhausted.

You don’t have to frame it as “Ramzan vs Shreya.” You can be deeply there for her *and* protect your fast, energy, prayers, and limits.

A few options that might help:

- **If the dance is after iftar:** you could say yes, but negotiate the terms — shorter routine, less intense choreography, comfortable outfit, no rehearsal on fasting days, breaks, water/food before performance.
- **If it’s before iftar:** maybe suggest you do a lighter symbolic opening with her — walk in together, a short duet, a chair dance, a group number where you’re featured but not carrying it.
- **Delegate the heavy lifting:** “I’ll co-direct and make sure it’s beautiful, but I need someone else to be the main opening dancer.”
- **Be honest without making it a debate:** not “I don’t want to,” but “I’m so excited for you, and I’m also worried I won’t be physically able to do the opening dance while fasting.”

You could tell her something like:

> “Shreya, I want you to know I’m all in for you. But I’m feeling nervous because Ramzan and fasting will affect my energy. I don’t want to promise the opening dance and then disappoint you or feel awful. Can we plan something that lets me be part of the opening in a way I can actually manage?”

That way you’re not rejecting her — you’re protecting the friendship from a last-minute crash.

And honestly, being the co-director is already a huge act of love. You are allowed to not perform at full force too. You can be the person who makes her night magical without sacrificing your own wellbeing to prove it.

Yesterday she said, with total love, "one day of fasting won't matter na, I'll feed you myself." She wasn't being mean — she just doesn't know what she's asking. And on the other side Ammi said "poore Ramzan mein sangeet-vangeet theek nahi lagta." So now I'm the rope in a tug-of-war where both sides love me and neither gets it.

Yaar, that “one day of fasting won’t matter na” line — even said with love — must have landed so badly. Because for you it’s not “one day of hunger.” It’s worship, discipline, intention, energy, your relationship with Allah. And then Ammi’s side is like, “this whole thing doesn’t feel right.” So you’re stuck between *my best friend needs me* and *my faith/family needs me* — and nobody is seeing the actual knot in your chest.

The key thing: **you don’t have to make Shreya understand Ramzan perfectly for your boundary to be valid.** And you don’t have to make Ammi fully approve of the sangeet for your love for Shreya to be real.

You can separate the conversations.

To Shreya, maybe:

> “Shreya, I know you’re saying it with love, and I know how much this opening dance means to you. But fasting isn’t just ‘not eating for one day’ for me. I’m worried I won’t have the energy, and I don’t want to promise you something and then fail you on the day. I’m still all in for you — I’ll help direct, plan, make it beautiful — but can we make the opening something I can actually manage? Maybe shorter, after iftar, or me walking in with you instead of doing the full dance?”

If she says again, “Arre one day won’t matter,” you can gently hold the line:

> “I know it feels that way to you. But for me it matters. Please don’t make me choose between disappointing you and compromising something important to me.”

To Ammi, maybe:

> “Ammi, I hear you. I’m also thinking about Ramzan and what feels right. But Shreya isn’t just any friend — we’ve planned this since we were kids. I don’t want to be careless with my fast or my deen. I’m trying to go in a way that feels respectful and not overdo it.”

And privately, ask yourself: **what is the line you don’t want to cross?**  
Not “what will make everyone happy?” Because everyone may not be happy.

Maybe the answer is: attend, help direct, skip the dance.  
Maybe: do a tiny symbolic opening after iftar.  
Maybe: don’t go at all.  
Maybe: go but leave before things get too late/food-heavy.

But please don’t let love become a trap where you have to prove devotion by emptying your own cup. You can be Shreya’s person without performing at full volume while fasting. You can honor Ramzan without abandoning your friend. Both truths can exist.

Honestly I'm so tired that I've started drafting the escape: I tell Shreya there's an office deployment that week, do a video call appearance, send a big gift. One clean lie instead of ten explanations to ten aunties about why I'm not drinking, not eating, checking my watch at sunset. She'd never know. Tell me that's not terrible?

No — it’s not “terrible” that your brain is drafting an escape hatch. That’s exhaustion talking. That’s you trying to find a way out of a situation where every option feels like betraying someone.

But I don’t think the office-deployment lie will feel clean for long. It might save you from ten aunties, yes — but it could leave you feeling guilty with Shreya too, especially because this isn’t just any event. And if she ever finds out, she may not hear “I was overwhelmed”; she may hear “you invented a reason not to be there.”

You don’t need ten explanations. You need one short, loving boundary.

To Shreya, maybe:

> “Shreya, I need to say this properly because I love you. I’m struggling with the sangeet because it’s during Ramzan and I’ll be fasting. I don’t think I can do the opening dance the way you deserve. I’m still all in for you — I’ll help plan, coordinate, be there for the parts I can — but I can’t promise a full dance.”

If she says, “But one day won’t matter,” you can say:

> “I know you mean it lovingly. But it does matter to me. Please don’t make me feel guilty for taking my fast seriously.”

And for aunties? You owe them almost nothing.

> “I’m fasting, so I’m keeping it low-key.”  
> “I’ll eat after sunset, thank you.”  
> “No need, I’m good.”  
> “I’m just here to support Shreya.”

That’s it. No courtroom defense.

Also: you’re allowed to choose a smaller version of showing up. Not fake office deployment. Not full dramatic confession. Just: “I can come for X hours,” “I’ll help from behind the scenes,” “I’ll do a video call,” “I won’t do the dance,” “I’ll leave at iftar.”

The goal isn’t to make everyone understand. It’s to stop turning yourself into the rope.

And under all of it there's this small stone in my chest — this is the first time in eighteen years of friendship that my deen and her big day have actually collided. If I get this wrong, one of two things I love gets a permanent dent. Her shaadi photos will exist forever, and so will my Ramzan. I don't want to be a sad story in either album.

That “small stone” makes so much sense.

Because this isn’t really about one dance, one night, one meal. It’s the first time eighteen years of love and your deen are standing in the same doorway asking, “Which one of us are you choosing?” And of course that feels terrifying.

But I don’t think choosing your fast means choosing against Shreya.

You can say to her — maybe with tears, maybe very simply:

> “Shreya, I love you so much. This is your big day, and I want to be there for you. But I’m also scared because this is Ramzan, and my fast matters deeply to me. I don’t want to lie, disappear, or promise something I can’t give. I need your help making space for both — your wedding and my deen.”

That sentence is important: **you need her help too.** Not just her permission. Her help.

And if she loves you the way you love her, she may be disappointed — but she can survive being disappointed. Disappointment doesn’t mean you’ve broken the friendship. A real friend can hold some disappointment and still understand.

As for the albums: Shreya’s photos don’t need you to be glowing, eating, drinking, dancing full-out to prove you were there. They can show you beside her, supporting her, loving her. And your Ramzan doesn’t become a sad story because you set a boundary. It may become the Ramzan where you stopped performing devotion for everyone and actually protected it.

You don’t have to make this collision beautiful. You just have to make sure you don’t lie to yourself to keep the peace.

The cleanest path may be messy conversation, not a clean lie.  
But messy truth won’t leave a dent the way betrayal — even a lovingly packaged one — might.
